reconcile.note: Keil and Delitzsch read Ner in 1 Chronicles as a remote ancestor of Kish, not his immediate father, since Hebrew genealogies often skip intervening generations.

discrepancy.note: Wellhausen and Spinoza treat Chronicles' divergences from Samuel-Kings as a mark of the Chronicler's own late reworking, of which Kish's two fathers is one instance.

quotes.text: When the narrative of Chronicles runs parallel with the older historical books of the canon, it makes no real additions, but the tradition is merely differently coloured, under the influence of contemporary motives.
quotes.attr: Julius Wellhausen (d. 1918), Prolegomena to the History of Israel (1885), on the Chronicler's habitual recoloring of parallel Samuel-Kings material.

quotes.text: the Chronicler has produced this picture of old Israel, so different in outline and colour from the genuine tradition, not of his own suggestion and on his own responsibility, but on the ground of documents that lay before him.
quotes.attr: Julius Wellhausen (d. 1918), Prolegomena to the History of Israel (1885), on the Chronicler's systematic departure from the older tradition's picture of Israel.

quotes.text: Anyone who compares the narratives in Chronicles with the narratives in the books of Kings, will find many similar discrepancies.
quotes.attr: Benedict de Spinoza (d. 1677), A Theologico-Political Treatise, Part II (1883 trans.), on the general run of discrepancies between Chronicles and Samuel-Kings.

sides.snippet: whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel, the son of Zeror
sides.verseText: Now there was a man of Benjamin, whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel, the son of Zeror, the son of Becorath, the son of Aphiah, the son of a Benjamite, a mighty man of valor.

sides.snippet: Ner became the father of Kish; and Kish became the father of Saul
sides.verseText: Ner became the father of Kish; and Kish became the father of Saul; and Saul became the father of Jonathan, and Malchishua, and Abinadab, and Eshbaal.
